newsitem.title: PERU: Hostages in Peru show courage and endurance.
newsitem.headline: Hostages in Peru show courage and endurance.

text.p: Clad in elegant suits, 400 ministers, judges, generals and diplomats from around the world are surviving on fruit and water in the Japanese embassy in Lima, wondering who will be the first victim of rebels threatening to kill them unless their demands are met.
Two days after armed guerrillas from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed the lavish embassy compound, members of Lima's diplomatic elite are sharing just four bathrooms.
Details are scant about the situation inside the embassy, which lies in the posh San Isidro neighbourhood close to Lima's Pacific coast.
High walls surround the white building. The tip of a red and white party tent -- erected for the party to celebrate the Japanese Emperor's birthday -- can just be seen over the barriers.
Hostages' relatives, along with reporters and diplomats, camp at either end of the tree-lined street, trying to snatch a few minutes of sleep as their vigil continues.

"They will start to kill people. The government must do something, please," said Elizabeth Canales, who was released with a group of about 80 women and elderly people late on Tuesday but whose husband remains inside.
Fears soared on Thursday when two shots were heard from inside the compound. But there were no immediate reports of any injuries, and shortly afterward four more male captives were freed.

Four ambassadors released earlier as "hostages on parole" have been acting as mediators with the radical rebels inside, whose captives still include Peru's ministers of foreign affairs and agriculture and supreme court president.
The Canadian embassy, whose ambassador is one of the mediators, said in a communique the hostages are "exhibiting qualities of courage and endurance."

They have to stand in long lines to use the bathrooms and many of them were suffering head- and stomach-aches. Rebels allowed the Red Cross to hand them medicine, including drugs for heart ailments, asthma and insulin.

The leftist guerrillas, who are demanding the release of 400 to 500 jailed comrades and talks with President Alberto Fujimori, also allowed bananas, apples, pears, juice and about 200 gallons (750 litres) of drinking water to be handed in to the captives.
But the water supply is likely to remain short.
"I doubt any of them could have taken a shower in the last two days," one fireman on the scene said.

Outside the embassy, small groups of onlookers discussed in low voices how the standoff might end. Some expected negotiations to resolve the situation, but others were less optimistic, saying the rebels had no other way than violence, "as they were already dead men."
